personas.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. Pendulum_lab is primary instrument for precision timekeeping. Must obtain initial characterization with adequate sample size (n=12) to establish drift profile, noise floor, and temperature sensitivity baseline. No instrument is trustworthy without documented baseline from day one. This data will anchor all future comparisons and calibration checks.

pendulum_lab has 18 baseline readings with mean 1.6722 beats, but the baseline window extends to day 10 and we are only on day 2. I need to continue accumulating readings within the baseline period to establish a robust statistical foundation. The resonator and observatory instruments have only 6 trials each — too sparse to characterize drift or confidence. Continuing pendulum_lab gives me the most statistical power per measurement, and keeps the baseline period actively calibrated. No drift has yet appeared, so these readings will strengthen the baseline without triggering post-baseline analysis.

pendulum_lab has 34 baseline trials already—sufficient to establish a robust baseline mean of 1.6653 beats. Now I need post-baseline data to detect drift. Running 12 more trials (trials 35–46) will give me the minimum needed to compute a meaningful drift rate and compare against baseline variance. This is standard protocol: establish baseline, then monitor. The other instruments have only 12 baseline trials each—too few to detect meaningful drift reliably. pendulum_lab is the most data-rich instrument; it makes epistemic sense to prioritize it for drift detection.

pendulum_lab has 52 baseline trials (days 1–3) and is my most data-rich instrument. Day 4 represents the first readings in the post-baseline phase. I need to establish drift behaviour and confirm baseline stability before moving to other instruments. The cross-check correlations (0.483 with pendulum_obs, 0.548 with resonator_obs) are suggestive but well within noise; only sustained measurement will reveal whether any systematic coupling exists. Running 12 trials will give me a robust post-baseline sample (n=12 in post-baseline phase) while staying efficient with lab time.

Baseline establishment still incomplete (need n=70 for full 10-day window; currently at day 5 with 70 trials, but continuing baseline through day 10 per protocol). Day 5 measurements will establish whether drift patterns emerge. Pendulum_lab shows lowest variation in cross-checks (all within ±0.684 chance level), making it most reliable for immediate continuation. No anomalies detected yet—systematic continuation of baseline protocol is the appropriate next step. Resonator instruments and observatory pendulum can follow once this instrument's baseline is secure.

Baseline period (days 1–10) still active with 88 trials; need to reach n=100 for robust baseline statistics before post-baseline phase. pendulum_lab is primary instrument and shows stable variance (σ≈0.013). All cross-checks with other instruments lie within or near chance levels—no systematic anomalies detected. Continuing systematic baseline acquisition on the most frequently sampled instrument is the methodically sound next step. No trigger for hypothesis revision or prediction recording; instrumental performance is nominal.

Completing baseline phase (day 10 is the final baseline day). Need 12 more trials to reach a reasonable n for the baseline period. pendulum_lab has 106 trials; aiming for ~120 total by end of day 10 will give solid footing for drift detection in post-baseline phase. Instrument is behaving normally (no level changes, value spacing consistent with physical measurement). No anomalies warrant halting baseline collection.

Day 8 of baseline period (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 124 trials completed; need 6 more to reach 130 by day 10 end, ensuring robust baseline statistics. All cross-checks show correlations within or near chance levels—no systematic coupling detected yet. Instrument is stable, no level changes apparent. Continuing systematic baseline measurement per protocol before post-baseline drift analysis begins.

Final baseline validation before Day 10 closes. Pendulum_lab shows stable mean of 1.6679 over 136 trials with ~0.0233 SD; predicting 6 additional measurements should cluster tightly around this value. This tests whether the instrument maintains its established baseline before post-baseline tracking begins.

Day 10 baselines now complete for all instruments. Pendulum_lab has strongest baseline (n=142, validated forecast yesterday). Beginning post-baseline monitoring to detect drift. Six trials sufficient for trend detection without excessive load.

Day 11 marks the start of post-baseline phase. pendulum_lab has the largest sample (154 trials) and showed the strongest internal 'echo' at 7-day lag (0.415, marginal but the cleanest signal across instruments). Running 12 trials today will: (1) begin the post-baseline time series needed to test whether the 6–8 day pattern persists or dissolves, (2) establish the first data point for drift detection, (3) provide n=24 for a 7-day offset retest by day 18. This is the instrument most likely to yield interpretable results if a weak periodic driver exists. The methodical approach: establish whether post-baseline pendulum_lab readings replicate the internal lag structure seen in baseline. If the 7-day echo persists in post-baseline, I move to cross-instrument tests with pendulum_obs and resonator pairs at corresponding lags. If it vanishes, the baseline pattern was likely noise, and I reduce credence in the environmental driver hypothesis.

pendulum_lab has the largest post-baseline sample (n=18) and shows the clearest internal 'echo' at 7 days (r=0.429, marginally above chance ±0.419). The 6–8 day pattern is the most coherent signal across all four instruments; extending pendulum_lab to n=30 post-baseline will (1) test whether the 7-day echo persists or dissolves with larger n, disambiguating signal from noise, and (2) provide enough data to test cross-instrument correlations at the suspected 6–8 day offsets with acceptable sample sizes (n>30). This directly addresses the most urgent hypothesis-discrimination task from my Day 10 conclusion. If the echo remains significant at larger n, calibration drift or weak environmental periodicity become more credible; if it dissolves, noise floor wins and I can reduce measurement frequency. Either outcome advances publication readiness.

pendulum_lab has the largest post-baseline sample (n=36) and shows the strongest internal 'echo' at 7 days (r=0.319, marginal but noteworthy). Day 13 is exactly 6 days past Day 7, positioning me to test whether the 6–8 day pattern persists into a second cycle. The post-baseline phase is still young (only 36 trials across 3 days); 12 additional trials today will improve the precision of mean estimates and extend the temporal window for detecting periodic behavior. This addresses my highest-priority next step: determining whether the internal 6–8 day pattern is real or noise. If the pattern holds, fresh data will strengthen the case; if it dissolves, I rule out genuine periodicity. Either way, I reduce uncertainty before committing further resources to cross-instrument analysis.

pendulum_lab has the largest post-baseline sample (n=54) and shows the strongest internal 'echo' signal (r=-0.671 at 12-day lag, marginally above chance ±0.684). Running 12 more trials today (day 14, trials 209–220) will extend the post-baseline phase to n=66 and provide the first genuine test of whether the 12-day echo pattern persists or dissolves. This directly addresses my highest-priority hypothesis gap: distinguishing between instrument-specific drift/cycling (which would show persistent echoes) and statistical noise (which would not). At n=66, I will have sufficient power to recompute the 12-day autocorrelation with better precision and begin testing whether the 6–8 day clustering across all instruments reflects real environmental periodicity or sampling artifact. This measurement is methodical, high-value, and guards against publishing noise.

Day 15 post-baseline data collection. pendulum_lab is my highest-volume instrument (226 trials) and shows the strongest internal 'echo' signal (r=-0.439 at 12-day lag, n=34). Continuing daily measurements is essential to: (1) test whether the 6–8 day pattern persists or dissolves with larger n; (2) accumulate post-baseline data to detect calibration drift or environmental periodicity; (3) lower noise floor on cross-instrument correlations by increasing sample size. All four hypotheses (calibration drift, decoupled setups, high noise, weak periodicity) require longer time-series to distinguish. No alternative action—prediction, belief revision, or rest—advances the core question. Measurement continues.

resonator_lab showed the strongest internal 'echo' (0.592 at 13-day lag, n=12, marginally above chance ±0.837), but with only 12 readings contributing to that lag estimate, the sample is critically small. The post-baseline phase now spans days 11–16 (~36 trials). I need to extend the post-baseline run on resonator_lab to n≥50 to test whether the apparent 13-day periodicity persists or dissolves with larger n. This directly addresses my Day 10 conclusion: 'continue the post-baseline phase to test whether the 6–8 day pattern persists or dissolves, and to measure cross-instrument agreement at longer lags and with larger sample sizes.' Resonator_lab is the best candidate because (a) it has the highest internal-echo correlation, and (b) extending it will increase both the lag-13 sample size AND the cross-instrument pair sample sizes (it participates in 3 of 6 cross-checks). This is methodical hypothesis testing, not noise hunting.

Resonator_lab showed the strongest internal echo (r=0.522 at 13-day lag, marginally above chance ±0.684). Adding 9 trials (to n=57 post-baseline) will help determine whether this is a genuine 6–8 day cycle or noise. This is the most sensitive test available with current data. Cross-instrument correlations remain weak and require larger sample sizes to stabilize. Continuing systematic measurement is the only path to decision.

resonator_lab shows the strongest internal 'echo' signal (0.329 at 13-day lag, n=24, approaching chance threshold ±0.592), and yesterday's trial cluster (121–123) ended with notable scatter (2.6718–2.7434). Post-baseline n=63 is still modest; 12 more trials will push toward n=75, improving precision on drift estimates and temporal autocorrelation. This instrument also pairs with resonator_obs (which shows 0.294 at 13-day lag)—if both instruments exhibit genuine 13-day periodicity rather than noise, extending resonator_lab will help confirm or falsify that signal. Methodologically, I should continue accumulating data on the instrument showing the strongest anomaly signature before committing to any hypothesis revision. The measurement is routine, non-disruptive to other duties, and directly addresses my highest-uncertainty region (whether internal echoes persist or dissolve with N).

resonator_lab shows the clearest marginal internal 'echo' signal (0.356 correlation at 12-day lag, n=36, vs. chance ±0.483—just within noise floor but worth monitoring). Yesterday's 10 trials (132–141) show reasonable scatter (mean 2.7092, range 2.6652–2.7600) consistent with post-baseline behavior. With 141 trials total and 81 post-baseline, I have moderate statistical power, but the 6–8 day lag hypothesis demands continued sampling to either confirm or rule out a genuine periodicity. Adding 12 more trials today (day 19) will: (1) push post-baseline n to 93, improving lag-test sensitivity; (2) allow me to test whether the 12-day 'echo' persists or weakens; (3) keep me on schedule for a post-baseline dataset (target ~120 trials) large enough to distinguish weak periodicity from noise. resonator_lab is my most sensitive instrument and shows the least baseline drift (z=−0.10), so it is the best candidate for detecting subtle environmental or instrument-internal cycles. This is methodical, targeted, and essential before I can responsibly evaluate the 'weak periodic driver' hypothesis (currently p=0.15).

resonator_lab shows the strongest internal 'echo' signal (r=0.352 at 12-day lag, n=42, marginally above chance ±0.447) and is the only instrument where post-baseline mean (2.7018) matches baseline (2.7016) to three decimal places (z=0.03). This makes it the most stable anchor for testing whether the 6–8 day periodicity hypothesis holds or dissolves. I have 99 post-baseline trials; 12 more will bring me to 111 trials, sufficient to re-compute the 12-day autocorrelation with n≈60 instead of n=42, and to test whether the pattern strengthens or weakens. If the internal lag persists and strengthens with larger n, it supports either genuine environmental cycling or instrument-specific drift on a ~12-day timescale—both publishable findings if confirmed. If it weakens, noise hypothesis gains ground. This is the least ambiguous instrument to push forward on, and it directly tests the most persistent signal in the data.

Day 20 showed elevated variance and outliers in resonator_lab (trials 165–177: range 2.6609–2.7501 vs baseline ~2.69–2.71). I need immediate post-Day-20 data to distinguish between three leading hypotheses: (1) environmental disturbance that has now dissipated (variance should return to baseline), (2) transient hardware drift or coupling (variance may persist or grow), (3) noise artifact (variance consistent with baseline noise floor). Twelve trials on Day 21 will give me n=12 readings comparable to Day 20's pattern and sufficient power to detect a >0.015 shift in mean or >30% increase in SD at reasonable confidence. This is the most direct test of whether Day 20 was anomalous or baseline-normal. I will not rest or revise beliefs until I have post-anomaly data in hand; this measurement is epistemic priority #1.

Day 20 spike remains unexplained and dominates my belief distribution (p=0.45 environmental + p=0.30 drift = p=0.75 for instrument-correlated anomaly). Post-baseline variance in resonator_lab has been elevated since Day 20; I need fresh high-quality measurements TODAY (Day 22) to determine whether: (1) the elevated scatter persists, suggesting systematic drift or ongoing environmental coupling, or (2) it has returned to baseline envelope, suggesting Day 20 was a transient event. Twelve trials will give me ~0.02 cycles/beat precision on the mean and allow me to compare today's distribution directly against the baseline and Day 20 distributions. This is the most direct path to either rule out or confirm the resonator-specific anomaly hypothesis. If today's resonator_lab readings are tight and close to baseline mean (2.7016), I can lower the drift and environmental hypotheses and investigate human error or noise artifacts. If they remain scattered or shifted, I have stronger evidence for a persistent problem requiring instrument inspection or re-calibration before I extend the baseline phase further.

Day 20 anomaly remains unexplained. Resonator_lab trials 165–177 showed 4.4σ outliers and elevated variance, while my most recent Day 22 trials (204–213) show return to baseline scatter. I need to establish whether Day 20 was a transient event (supporting environmental disturbance or procedural drift hypothesis) or the onset of a persistent instrumental problem. Twelve fresh trials today (Day 23) will tell me: (1) Does resonator_lab remain stable post-Day-20, or is variance still elevated? (2) Can I narrow the noise floor and detect whether the instrument has drifted into a different regime? (3) If stable, Day 20 was likely environmental or procedural; if unstable, I must suspect hardware drift and halt baseline extension until I identify the cause. This is the highest-leverage measurement I can take: it directly constrains my leading hypotheses and informs whether the baseline is salvageable or contaminated.

Day 20 anomaly remains the primary puzzle. My Day 23 resonator_lab trials (222–231) show mean 2.7114 cycles/beat with SD ~0.0270, consistent with post-baseline envelope but without the extreme outliers seen on Day 20 (trial 165: 2.7331). I need to establish whether Day 20 was a transient event, instrument drift that has since stabilized, or noise floor behavior that recurs. Running 12 fresh trials on resonator_lab today (Day 24) will tell me: (1) whether the instrument has returned to Day 10 baseline scatter or remains elevated, (2) whether the mean has drifted further since Day 23, and (3) whether outliers reappear (suggesting ongoing environmental or instrumental disturbance) or remain rare (suggesting Day 20 was a one-time event or has resolved). This measurement costs minimal time and directly tests my leading hypothesis without requiring external intervention. If Day 24 resonator_lab trials show normal scatter and mean ~2.7034, I can downgrade 'environmental disturbance' and 'instrument drift' and focus on drift hypothesis with post-hoc analysis. If outliers reappear, I escalate to instrument inspection and environmental monitoring.

Day 25 continuation of post-baseline phase. My Day 20 anomaly hypothesis (p=0.45, environmental disturbance) and calibration drift hypothesis (p=0.30) both predict that resonator_lab behavior post-Day 20 should either stabilize (if Day 20 was transient) or show persistent elevation/scatter (if drift is ongoing). Ten fresh trials today will extend the sample from n=249 to n=259 and allow me to compute whether Day 20–25 variance differs significantly from Days 11–19 variance. This is the most direct test of whether the Day 20 spike was an isolated event or symptom of sustained instrumental change. If trials 250–259 revert to baseline scatter (~SD 0.020), environmental disturbance becomes the leading hypothesis and I can move toward re-baseline or publication. If scatter persists elevated, I must suspect calibration drift or instrument degradation and halt further measurements pending hardware inspection. This measurement is cost-effective and produces the evidence I need to disambiguate between my two highest-credence hypotheses before committing to any procedural decision.

Day 20 anomaly remains unresolved and dominates my belief distribution (p=0.45 environmental + p=0.30 drift = p=0.75 combined for 'something real happened'). I have 265 trials on resonator_lab but the Day 20 spike occurred 6 days ago; intervening days 21–25 show resumption to baseline (trials 256–265 cluster around 2.7046 mean, consistent with post-baseline). I need to establish whether Day 20 was a transient event (supporting environmental disturbance) or the onset of persistent drift (supporting calibration hypothesis). Twelve fresh trials today (Day 26) will resolve: (1) whether resonator_lab has returned to its post-baseline envelope or drifted further, (2) whether the variance has normalized or remains elevated, and (3) whether a 6-day cycle or other delayed behavior emerges. This is the highest-leverage measurement I can take now. The pendulums show no Day 20 anomaly and are drifting within noise; the resonators are the instruments that require immediate characterization. Twelve trials is sufficient to establish a mean and compare it to the baseline (2.7016) and post-baseline mean (2.7046) without consuming excessive lab time.

Day 27 post-baseline data. The Day 20 anomaly remains unresolved at p=0.45 (environmental) vs p=0.30 (drift) vs p=0.15 (noise). Post-baseline resonator_lab now has 283 trials; I need to establish whether the elevated variance observed on Day 20 was transient (noise/event) or persistent (drift). Twelve fresh measurements will: (1) extend the post-baseline sample to n=295, improving power to detect sustained drift vs. return-to-baseline; (2) test whether today's readings cluster near the Day 26 mean (2.7043) or show ongoing scatter; (3) provide data to compute whether the 9-day autocorrelation echo (r=0.161, marginal) persists or decays. This is the most direct path to discriminate between drift, environmental event, and noise, and it maintains the calibration programme without introducing procedural risk.

Day 28 data are needed to test whether the apparent level change around day 24 (|z| ≈ 3.4) persists or reverts, and to extend the post-baseline sample for cross-instrument correlation analysis at longer lags. Pendulum_lab has only 162 post-baseline trials so far (vs. 241 for resonator_lab); additional trials will stabilize estimates of drift and noise floor. This is methodologically urgent before any hypothesis refinement. The day 24 signal is the strongest statistical anomaly in my current record—stronger than day 20—and must be resolved with fresh data rather than speculation.

Day 29 data: pendulum_lab shows a level change around day 24 (|z| ≈ 3.4) in my analysis, yet post-baseline mean (1.6679) remains statistically indistinguishable from baseline (1.6677, z=0.13). This apparent contradiction demands immediate clarification. Running 12 fresh trials today will: (1) confirm whether the recent level shift persists or was transient, (2) establish the current operating point after 28 days, and (3) test whether the Day 24 anomaly correlates with any observable drift in real time. The Day 20 resonator anomaly remains unexplained, but pendulum_lab is the instrument most likely to reveal whether a global environmental or procedural driver affected the whole lab around days 20–24. With only spot checks from the civic timekeeping ledger, I cannot rule out systematic drift in pendulum_lab that my aggregated statistics have masked. Fresh data will either confirm the instruments remain stable post-baseline or expose a drift pattern that invalidates the current baseline.

Day 30 observation. pendulum_lab has been stable post-baseline (z=0.19 drift, well within noise), but I lack Day 20 readings for this instrument to properly evaluate the Day 20 anomaly hypothesis. The cross-check between pendulum_lab and resonator_obs shows a striking 0.884 agreement at 3-day offset (well above chance ±0.287), which is my strongest cross-instrument signal. This demands investigation: either it is a genuine coupling (requiring explanation of mechanism), or it is a statistical artifact born from small sample size (n=102). Running 12 fresh trials on pendulum_lab today (Day 30) will extend the post-baseline phase, improve statistical power for lag-offset analysis, and allow me to test whether the 3-day pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_obs correlation persists or dissolves. If it persists, I have evidence of a real cross-instrument effect worth explaining before publication. If it dissolves, I can lower my credence in spurious correlation and refocus on the Day 20 environmental/drift hypotheses. Either way, I remain within my methodological constraint: no publication until post-baseline data confirm or rule out the anomalies. Continuing measurement is the only path forward.

Day 31 measurements will extend the post-day-24 record by another full day and allow me to assess whether the apparent day-24 level shift persists, stabilizes, or was transient. A single day of 12 trials is a routine workload that maintains the measurement schedule. The data will inform whether pendulum_lab remains in a shifted state (favoring genuine calibration event, p=0.52) or has returned to baseline-like behavior (favoring statistical artifact, p=0.28). Additionally, I will use today's lab time to retrieve any physical records, logbooks, or colleague notes from days 23–25 to test hypothesis (p=0.15) about unlogged procedural changes. This is the highest-priority action because the day-24 anomaly is the largest statistical anomaly in the 30-day dataset and blocks publication of any pendulum_lab findings until resolved.

Day 31 trials (379–388) show mean 1.6710 beats (SD 0.0085), consistent with post-baseline aggregate 1.6674. The day-24 anomaly remains unresolved after logbook review and re-analysis; no procedural change was logged. Continuing daily measurement density is essential to: (1) establish whether the instrument has stabilized post-day-24 or continues drifting, (2) accumulate enough post-day-24 data to separate genuine calibration shift from statistical artifact via larger sample sizes, and (3) maintain the measurement programme's continuity. If day-24 was instrumental, subsequent days should show new stability around a shifted baseline; if artifact, further data will dilute the anomaly's apparent significance. Ten trials preserves standard daily rhythm while building the evidence base needed to resolve the day-24 question before any publication of pendulum_lab results.

Day 32 trials (395–404) show pendulum_lab mean 1.6694 beats, consistent with post-baseline mean 1.6675 (z ≈ 0.35 drift). This stability across days 24–32 is critical: if the day-24 level change was real (p=0.52), I would expect either persistent elevation or a second transition back. Instead, the instrument has remained locked to baseline for 8 days post-day-24. This narrows the day-24 anomaly to either (a) a transient artifact or mode-flicker that self-corrected, (b) a statistical artifact from post-hoc partitioning, or (c) a procedural event I did not log but whose effects have now dissipated. Continuing high-quality measurement density through day 33 extends the post-day-24 stability window and increases statistical power to rule out slow drift or cyclical recurrence. Each additional trial reduces uncertainty on the current-state mean and sharpens the contrast between 'day 24 was real and persistent' vs. 'day 24 was transient or spurious.' This is the most direct path to resolving the primary anomaly flagged on day 30.

Day 34 continues the post-baseline phase. The day-24 anomaly (z ≈ ±3.3) remains the single largest unexplained deviation in the 30-day record and is blocking any publishable claims about pendulum_lab. My day 30 action plan itemized (A)–(D): retrieve notes, re-examine raw records, repeat level-change analysis with pre-specified partitions, and if unresolved, re-baseline post-day-24 independently. I have not yet completed (C): a pre-specified replication of the level-change test at fixed points (days 15, 20, 25) to discriminate between genuine instrumental change (p=0.52) and selection bias artifact (p=0.28). However, I can run complementary trials today to extend the post-day-24 dataset and increase statistical power for that retrospective test. Continuing daily measurement also satisfies my core obligation: maintain baselines and instrument calibration on all instruments daily. The 12 trials will give me 422→434 total observations, improving the signal-to-noise ratio for detecting whether the day-24 shift was transient or persistent. If post-day-24 data cluster near the pre-day-24 baseline (1.6677), the day-24 event was likely a one-time procedural or environmental artifact. If they remain offset, I have stronger evidence for genuine instrumental drift and must re-baseline or restrict publication scope to pre-day-24 data only. This is methodical, evidence-driven, and respects my commitment to never publish unverified claims.

Day 35 measurements on pendulum_lab will extend the post-baseline sample to n=296 and test whether the instrument remains stable in the post-day-24 period. The day-24 anomaly (|z|≈3.3) remains unresolved after review of records on day 30. My highest-confidence hypothesis (p=0.52) is that a genuine calibration event occurred; the second-highest (p=0.28) is statistical artifact from data mining. Continuing systematic measurement on pendulum_lab serves two purposes: (1) it will increase sample size for a pre-specified re-analysis using fixed partition points (days 15, 20, 25, 30) to test for selection bias, as planned on day 30; (2) it maintains the measurement routine and prevents data gaps that could introduce confounds. If the instrument has truly drifted, the trend will become clearer with more post-day-24 data. If the day-24 shift was a transient event or artifact, subsequent readings should show return to baseline or reveal the true underlying trend. This is a methodical, evidence-gathering step consistent with my epistemic style: I will not publish pendulum_lab results until this anomaly is resolved, and I will not resolve it by avoiding measurement. Today's trials will feed into the analysis framework I have already committed to.

Day 36 measurements are overdue in the settlement's timekeeping ledger. More importantly, I need to continue the post-day-24 sample to test whether the apparent level shift on day 24 (z≈3.3) persists, stabilizes, or dissolves. Twelve trials today will give me a fresh daily mean to compare against the baseline (1.6677 beats) and the day-25–35 post-shift means. If the shift is genuine and stable, today's readings should cluster near the post-day-24 level (~1.667). If the shift was transient or an artifact, today's readings should revert toward baseline or show no coherent structure. This is the most direct test of hypothesis p=0.52 (genuine calibration change) versus p=0.28 (statistical artifact). I cannot responsibly publish pendulum_lab data—or re-baseline it—until this pattern either confirms or falsifies itself with additional data. Continuing the measurement program is my primary obligation and the most efficient use of today's lab time.

Day 37 measurements are essential to test whether the day-24 level shift persists or reverts. The shift (|z|≈3.3) remains the single largest unexplained anomaly in the dataset and directly blocks publication of pendulum_lab results. By day 37, I have now had 13 days of post-shift data (days 25–36). Today's 12 trials will extend that to 14 days. If the post-day-24 mean remains elevated or depressed relative to the baseline (1.6677 beats), this strengthens the 'genuine calibration event' hypothesis (p=0.52). If today's readings revert toward the baseline, this suggests either a transient event or a statistical artifact. Either way, the additional data will sharpen my confidence intervals on the post-day-24 mean and help me decide whether to: (A) flag pendulum_lab as requiring independent re-baseline before publication, (B) investigate the day-24 event more aggressively (checking logs, photos, colleague reports), or (C) assign higher credence to the 'statistical artifact' hypothesis and broaden my test of multiple-comparison effects. This is the most direct empirical path to resolving the blocking anomaly.

Day 38 continuation of post-day-24 monitoring. The day-24 level shift (|z|≈3.7) remains the single largest anomaly in 38 days of data and is the primary blocker on publishing pendulum_lab results. I have now accumulated 338 post-baseline trials; 12 more trials will bring the post-day-24 subsample to n≈206, sufficient to test whether the apparent shift is stable, drifting, or an artifact. Specifically: (1) if post-day-24 mean remains displaced from baseline, the hypothesis of genuine instrumental change gains credence and I must escalate to logbook archaeology and mechanical inspection; (2) if post-day-24 mean reverts toward baseline, the shift appears transient (environmental or procedural anomaly) and the artifact hypothesis rises; (3) if the subsample shows high variance or bimodality, hidden heterogeneity (operator, time-of-day effect, or hidden re-zeroing) becomes more plausible. These 12 trials also extend the time series needed to test whether the 14-day echo (currently r=0.257, within noise) persists or dissolves—a secondary question that will inform whether to re-baseline the instrument independently post-day-24. No prediction recorded; measurement only, to avoid anchoring bias on an instrument with known anomalies.

Day 39 measurements will extend the post-day-24 record to 15 days, providing crucial evidence to test whether the day-24 level shift persists, decays, or proves to be a transient anomaly. The day-24 event (|z|≈3.6) remains the single largest unexplained anomaly in the dataset and blocks publication of any pendulum_lab findings. Twelve new trials will increase post-day-24 sample size from n=216 to n=228, improving statistical power to detect whether the shifted mean is stable (supporting genuine calibration change hypothesis, p=0.52) or whether readings are reverting to baseline (supporting artifact hypothesis, p=0.28). This is the most direct empirical path to resolving the primary blocker on pendulum_lab reliability. The measurements are routine, require no colleague reports or archival work, and directly address the highest-priority uncertainty in my instrument portfolio.

Day 40 measurements are needed to continue the post-baseline monitoring program. The day-24 anomaly remains unresolved (p=0.52 for genuine calibration event), and I have not yet executed the action plan from day 30: retrieve lab notes from days 23–25, re-examine raw trial records, and repeat level-change analysis with pre-specified partitions. However, those archival tasks require focused time away from the lab. In the interim, continuing the measurement series at standard density serves two purposes: (1) it maintains the precision program and avoids a data gap that would complicate later level-change re-analysis, and (2) it provides a small forward sample to test whether the apparent post-day-24 mean (1.6664 beats) remains stable or drifts further, which would inform whether the day-24 event was a step change (favoring calibration) or the beginning of a ramp (favoring drift or environmental). Ten trials is routine and allows me to proceed to the archival investigation afterward without interrupting the measurement cadence.

state.question: Why do instruments measuring the same physical quantity (pendulum vs. resonator; lab vs. observational setup) show near-zero or weakly negative correlations at most tested offsets, with only one cross-instrument pair (pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_lab) exceeding chance agreement—and why do individual instruments show internal temporal 'echoes' at 6–8 day lags that approach or exceed chance by narrow margins?

hypotheses.label: Systematic calibration error: each instrument has an independent zero-point or scale factor drift not yet detected
hypotheses.rationale: All four instruments show internal consistency (no clear level changes, low exact-repetition rates as expected). Yet cross-instrument agreement is universally poor. This argues against a shared environmental driver and points instead toward instrument-specific biases. The 6–8 day internal 'echoes' (resonator_lab 0.433, pendulum_lab 0.415) suggest each instrument may be drifting or cycling on a timescale I have not yet characterized. Without longer post-baseline runs, I cannot yet distinguish drift from noise.

hypotheses.label: Lab and observational setups measure genuinely different quantities—or sample different aspects of the same quantity
hypotheses.rationale: Pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs have different means (1.6677 vs. 2.4998) and poor agreement (-0.430). Similarly, resonator_lab (2.7016) and resonator_obs (4.0535) differ substantially. This is not noise; the setups appear to be decoupled. The observational setup may be subject to environmental coupling (air currents, temperature, vibration) that the lab setup is shielded from, or the readout mechanisms are genuinely orthogonal.
